data.description:
## The gap

S1 (`aa40`, change 2620) put the unreachable-scratch **refusal** in `gate_admission()`, which wraps
plan-review and completion-verifier. That is where ADR 0112 places it, and S1 implements the ADR
faithfully.

But the review-bot's per-review clone does **not** pass through `gate_admission()`. It is a plain
`tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix="reviewbot-")` following `TMPDIR`. So on a **declared-but-unmounted**
scratch volume, plan-review and completion-verifier correctly refuse — and the review-bot keeps
cloning onto the root filesystem, silently, which is precisely the outage this epic exists to prevent.

**This is a gap in the architecture, not a defect in S1.** AC3 only required the clone tempdir to
*resolve* to the volume, which it does via `TMPDIR`, and the ADR puts the refusal at gate admission.
S1's implementer flagged it rather than quietly widening scope, which was the right call.

## Why it matters more than it looks

The two paths differ in exactly the way that makes this dangerous:

- Plan-review and completion-verifier **refuse loudly** — an operator sees congestion errors and knows
  something is wrong.
- The review-bot **succeeds quietly** on the wrong disk. Nothing surfaces. The volume that was
  provisioned to hold these bytes sits empty while root fills, and the first symptom is the outage
  the epic was written to stop.

A partial refusal is arguably worse than none here, because the loud half creates confidence that the
protection is in force.

Note also the **two env vars** finding from S1, which is the same shape: `REBAR_GATE_TMPDIR` moves the
content-addressed store, while the review-bot clone follows `TMPDIR`. Setting only the first is half a
fix — and the clone is the path whose bytes scale linearly with concurrency.

## Required treatment

Per ADR 0069, a refusal on this path must get **retryable-deferral** treatment so it never becomes an
`LLM-Review −1`. A review-bot that votes −1 because a disk was unmounted would convert an
infrastructure fault into a false code-review verdict against an innocent change — the same
category error as a vacuous `Verified +1`.

## Acceptance criteria

Deterministic; verifiable in one run.

1. On a declared-but-unmounted scratch volume, the review-bot clone path **refuses** rather than
   falling back to root. Proven by the same two-marker mechanism S1 uses
   (`/var/lib/rebar/.gate-scratch-required` on root, `.gate-scratch-mounted` on the volume): only
   declaration-present + proof-absent refuses.
2. The refusal is a **retryable deferral** per ADR 0069, not an `LLM-Review −1`. Demonstrate that a
   review interrupted this way does not cast a negative vote.
3. **Defect-seeded:** with the declaration present and the proof absent, show the clone path creating
   nothing on the root filesystem — and show the pre-fix behaviour creating it. Assert on the absence
   of the directory, as S1's `test_the_refusal_creates_no_store_on_the_underlying_directory` does.
4. The no-op case is preserved: with no declaration present (the default, and every developer
   machine), nothing changes and no refusal occurs.
5. Monitoring and enforcement read the **same** proof marker, so they cannot disagree — S1 established
   that property for `observability.sh` and it must hold here too.

## Note for whoever takes this

Read change 2620 first. Its two-marker design exists because an unmounted volume raises **nothing** —
a mount point whose volume is absent is an ordinary, writable, empty directory, so a naive
`mkdir(parents=True)` silently recreates the store on root. Any fix here faces the identical trap.

## File impact

`src/rebar/review_bot/` (the clone path), and whichever module owns the scratch-availability check
S1 added to `src/rebar/llm/gate_admission.py` — the check should be shared, not reimplemented.
data.title: review-bot clone path bypasses the gate-scratch refusal: on a declared-but-unmounted volume it silently clones onto root while the gates correctly refuse
